name: Cyrus Cylinder
info: The Cyrus Cylinder is a clay cylinder inscribed in Akkadian cuneiform in the name of the Persian king Cyrus the Great, made as a foundation deposit in Babylon after its conquest in 539 BCE and found there in 1879.

facts.made: Made in the name of Cyrus the Great after the Persian conquest of Babylon; the familiar Babylonian wording suggests that Babylonian priests of Marduk composed it at Cyrus's behest
facts.form: A barrel-shaped cylinder of baked clay, 22.5 centimetres long and 10 centimetres across at its widest, bearing 45 surviving lines of Akkadian cuneiform in two main fragments, A and B
facts.where: The British Museum, London, which has displayed it since 1900; fragment B belongs to Yale University and is on loan to the museum
facts.known: a royal building inscription in the Mesopotamian tradition; the denunciation of Nabonidus; the claim that Marduk chose Cyrus; the restoration of temples and the return of deported peoples; later readings as a charter of human rights; a false translation circulated online

t: The Cylinder was a foundation deposit in the Babylonian tradition, made after the Persian conquest of 539 BCE, and its text reviles Nabonidus while presenting Cyrus as the king chosen by Marduk.
Biblical scholars long read it as confirming Cyrus's repatriation of the Jews, but it names only Mesopotamian sanctuaries and does not mention Jews, Jerusalem or Judea.
The Pahlavi government of Iran promoted it as the first charter of human rights; most historians regard that reading as anachronistic and see an ordinary royal building inscription.
dyk: A widely circulated translation that credits the Cylinder with abolishing slavery and guaranteeing a minimum wage and asylum is false: it makes claims that are not on the real cylinder and names the Zoroastrian god Ahura Mazda instead of Marduk.
ev: Cyrus conquered Babylon, after which the Cylinder was made and buried as a foundation deposit
Hormuzd Rassam found the Cylinder at Babylon, and Henry Rawlinson announced it to the Royal Asiatic Society in November
J. B. Nies of Yale University published the text of the smaller fragment, B
Fragment A was restored, re-fired and given plaster fillings
The Cylinder was displayed in Tehran for the celebration of 2,500 years of Persian monarchy
Fragments A and B were reunited at the British Museum
Two clay fragments in the museum since 1881 were identified as part of a tablet bearing the same text, and the Cylinder was lent again to Iran

sections.origins:
The Cylinder was made after the Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, when the Neo-Babylonian Empire was invaded by Cyrus and incorporated into his Persian Empire. It belongs to a long Mesopotamian practice. According to the British Museum, kings there had begun their reigns with declarations of reforms from as early as the third millennium BCE, and newly crowned kings of Babylon made public declarations of their own righteousness, often deposited in the foundations of public buildings. Such deposits included animal sacrifices, stone tablets, terracotta cones, cylinders and figures, and served to state a building's value, to commemorate the ruler or builder and to sanctify the building through an appeal for divine protection.

Earlier conquerors of Babylon had faced the same need to legitimise themselves. Marduk-apla-iddina II, who seized the throne in 722/1 BCE, declared that Marduk had chosen him, and Sargon II of Assyria, who conquered Babylon twelve years later, described how he honoured the gods and kept up their temples. Nabonidus, the king whom Cyrus deposed, had himself commissioned foundation texts on clay cylinders of the same basic formula. Cyrus's predecessor was an awkward figure: he came from the north of Babylonia, favoured the moon god Sin over Marduk and spent a long period in self-imposed exile.
sections.content:
The surviving inscription has 45 lines of Akkadian cuneiform in a formulaic style, which can be divided into six parts. Lines 1–19 revile Nabonidus and link Cyrus with the god Marduk; lines 20–22 give Cyrus's titles and genealogy and his peaceful entry into Babylon; lines 22–34 commend his policy of restoring Babylon; lines 34–35 are a prayer to Marduk for Cyrus and his son Cambyses; lines 36–37 declare that he enabled the people to live in peace and increased the offerings to the gods; and lines 38–45 describe his building works in Babylon.

The text charges Nabonidus with desecrating the temples and imposing forced labour on the people, and says that Marduk therefore abandoned Babylon and searched for an upright king. He took the hand of Cyrus, king of Anshan, and called him to the kingship. Midway through, the voice changes to the first person: Cyrus gives his titles, "king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad, king of the four quarters", in Mesopotamian rather than Persian style. He says that he restored peace, repaired ruined temples and their cults, returned sacred images and the former inhabitants whom Nabonidus had taken to Babylon, and rebuilt the city wall, within which he saw an inscription of Ashurbanipal. The remainder is missing.
sections.making:
The Cylinder is a barrel-shaped piece of baked clay, 22.5 centimetres long and 10 centimetres across at its widest. It was built in several stages around a cone-shaped clay core containing large grey stone inclusions, then given extra layers of clay to make it cylindrical and a fine surface slip on which the text was inscribed. It appears to have broken apart in antiquity. Its date is unclear: it is commonly said to belong to the early part of Cyrus's rule over Babylon, and the British Museum dates it between 539 and 530 BCE.

The text's use of long-established Babylonian themes has suggested that the priests of Marduk wrote it at Cyrus's request. It is close to another work of about the same time, the Verse Account of Nabonidus, which also attacks the former king and presents Cyrus as a liberator, and the two have been described as dependent on a common source. Morton Smith took that source to be propaganda spread by Cyrus's agents before the conquest; Simon J. Sherwin disputes this, holding that both are compositions written after the event from existing Mesopotamian themes. Hanspeter Schaudig has connected one line, in which Marduk saved Babylon from oppression, with a line of the Enûma Eliš, the Babylonian Epic of Creation.
sections.reception:
Readers have taken the Cylinder in several ways. Biblical scholars traditionally saw in it evidence for Cyrus's repatriation of the Jews, which the Book of Ezra attributes to him, because it speaks of returning deported peoples and restoring sanctuaries. Others point out that the passage lists only places in Mesopotamia and neighbouring regions and does not name Jews, Jerusalem or Judea. Amélie Kuhrt calls the context purely Babylonian, and Bob Becking concludes that it has nothing to do with Judeans, Jews or Jerusalem. Some scholars hold that Cyrus differed from earlier Assyrian and Babylonian rulers in sending captives home; others, among them R. J. van der Spek and Pierre Briant, note that the Assyrians did similar things.

The Pahlavi government of Iran promoted it as the first declaration of human rights. In 1971 Princess Ashraf Pahlavi gave a replica to the United Nations Secretary-General U Thant, and in 2010 Mahmoud Ahmadinejad also called it the first charter of human rights. Many historians call this reading anachronistic. C. B. F. Walker described it as simply a building inscription in the Babylonian and Assyrian tradition, and Arnold and Michalowski write that it is not an edict. The British Museum accepts that it does not proclaim human rights but describes the return of deported peoples as a significant reversal of earlier policy.
sections.survival:
Hormuzd Rassam found the Cylinder in March 1879, during excavations at Babylon for the British Museum under an Ottoman firman. It had been placed in the foundations of the Ésagila, the city's main temple. Rassam gave conflicting accounts of where it lay, once naming a mound near the village of Jumjuma and once Omran. Henry Rawlinson announced the find to the Royal Asiatic Society on 17 November 1879 and wrongly named Borsippa as its source. The text of the main body, fragment A, was restored in 1961, when it was re-fired and filled with plaster.

Fragment B was bought by J. B. Nies of Yale University from an antiquities dealer, and Nies published its text in 1920. Paul-Richard Berger identified it as part of the Cylinder in 1970, the fragments were reunited in 1972, and Yale lent B to the museum in exchange for "a suitable cuneiform tablet". In 2010 Wilfred Lambert and Irving Finkel recognised two fragments in the museum since 1881 as part of a tablet with the same text, which the museum took to show that the text was probably distributed widely across the Persian Empire. Two inscribed horse bones that surfaced in China in 1983 are now generally regarded as forgeries copied from an 1884 edition by E. A. Wallis Budge. Iran's press campaigned for the Cylinder's transfer in 1971, though it was obtained legally and found in modern Iraq.
sections.legacy:
The Cylinder has been displayed in the British Museum since 1900 and has been lent to Iran in 1971 and 2010, to Spain in 2006, to the United States in 2013 and to the Yale Peabody Museum in 2024. Many replicas have been made, some distributed by the Shah after 1971. The replica given to the United Nations has stood in its New York headquarters since then, and the United Nations continues to promote it as an ancient declaration of human rights.

Scholars disagree about its meaning. Neil MacGregor, a former director of the British Museum, called it the first attempt known to run a state of different nationalities and faiths, a new kind of statecraft, and also warned against narrowing its meaning to one political agenda, saying it is part of the history of the ancient Near East and of Mesopotamian kingship. Others, including Josef Wiesehöfer, see the portrayal of Cyrus as a champion of human rights as an illusion. The text also omits events that other sources record, among them the Battle of Opis, and historians such as Lisbeth Fried and Max Mallowan read its account of a peaceful welcome as conqueror's rhetoric. The Freedom Sculpture, a stainless steel work by Cecil Balmond in Century City, California, is modelled on it.

summary: The Cyrus Cylinder is a clay foundation deposit inscribed after Cyrus the Great's conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, found there in 1879. Its text follows Mesopotamian royal custom, and it has been read as evidence for the return of the Jews and as a charter of human rights, readings historians dispute.
references: Paul-Alain Beaulieu, The Reign of Nabonidus, King of Babylon (556-539 B.C.) (Yale University, 1986)
Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire (Eisenbrauns, 2006)
John Curtis, Forgotten Empire: The World of Ancient Persia (University of California Press, 2005)
